# Introduction

Factors such as crop yield, income and health outcomes can be heavily influenced by geography. This activity will serve as an introduction to including neighbors as predictors in an Ordinary Least Squares(OLS) model.

## Learning Goals

 - Review basic mapping and GIS skills in R
 - Understand different neighborhood structures and evaluate their costs and benefits
 - Visualize limitations of OLS when working with spatially correlated data
 - Introduce the methods of a spatial lag model
 - Use Moran's I as a method of evaluating the spatial correlation within the residuals of a model

## Load necessary packages

```{r}
#| message: FALSE
library(tidyverse)
library(sf) # package to use spatial features in R
library(tigris) # package with county boundaries
library(spdep) # package to create neighborhoods
library(spatialreg) # package to spatially model data

# Load in Data
# Using `USAboundaries` read in the shapefiles for states
countiesMN <- read_sf("data/counties_MN/counties_MN.shp")

crops <- read_csv("data/crop_production.csv") |> 
  filter(stateID == 27) |> 
  select(COUNTYFP = countyID, soybean, corn, wheat)

climate <- read_csv("data/climate_county.csv") |> 
  filter(state == "Minnesota") |> 
  select(COUNTYFP = ID3, precip = precip2125, temp = temp2125)
```

# 2. Methods for analyzing neighbors

In this section we will look at different neighborhood structures and ultimately decide what method to use going forward for this data. Ideally, we want counties to have a similar number of neighbors that seem reasonable to assume there would be correlation between the two. We also want to make sure that each county has some neighbors, so we have that data when we go to model.

## Rook and Queen Neighbors

This will assign neighbors based if the two regions share a point(Queen) or share a border(Rook). Using the spatial features, make a plot of the neighborhoods over the county map(no other variables). Comment on the difference(or lack thereof!) between the two neighborhood structures.

```{r}
#| eval: FALSE
# Find the center of each county
centroids <- st_centroid(st_geometry(countiesMN), of_largest_polygon = TRUE)

# Create neighborhood structures
queen_nb <- poly2nb(countiesMN, queen = TRUE)
rook_nb <- poly2nb(countiesMN, queen = FALSE)

# Convert Neighborhood Structure to shape files
queen_lines <- nb2lines(nb = queen_nb, coords = centroids, as_sf = TRUE)
rook_lines <- nb2lines(nb = rook_nb, coords = centroids, as_sf = TRUE)

# Map the neighborhoods
```


## K-Nearest Neighbors

Each region will be given at minimum K neighbors, the close K to its center. Choose a reasonable number of neighbors to give each region. Then plot the neighbors like previously. Comment on the costs and benefits to this structure compared to others.

```{r}
knn_lines <- nb2lines(nb = knn_nb, coords = centroids, as_sf = TRUE)
```


## Moran's I

Moran's I is a measure of spatial correlation. Below is code that calculates Moran's I for the residuals of each county and plots it. High magnitude Moran's I mean that the residuals are highly spatially correlated with those around it. Negative mean an inverse correlation, positive meaning that residuals are very similar. Moran's I cannot be calculated if a county has no neighbors, make sure that whatever neighborhood structure you chose, there was a neighbor for each county.

```{r}
#| eval: FALSE
# Turn neighborhood into list needed for model, using your chosen structure
nb_mat <- nb2listw(knn_nb, style = "W")

# Calculate Moran's I for each county
local_moran <- spdep::localmoran(joined_counties$resid, nb_mat)

# Plot Local Moran's I
joined_counties |> 
  bind_cols(local_moran) |> 
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = Ii)) +
  labs(fill = 'Local Moran I') + 
  scale_fill_gradient2(mid = "white", high = "red", low = "blue") +
  ggthemes::theme_map() +
  theme(legend.position = "right") 
```


# 4. Creating a Spatial Lag Model

Likely your map of residuals looked highly spatially correlated. Counties with low residuals were quite close to counties with high residuals. 

$Y = \rho \cdot W + \beta \cdot X + \epsilon$

This is the formula for the spatial lag model. The new term different from OLS is $\rho \cdot W$. $\rho$ is a weight, similar to $\beta$ and W is the matrix of our neighbors, row-standardized. This mean each row, which represents one county, will add up to 1. Now, we have our traditional OLS model, with a predictor added for the mean outcome of each of the counties neighbors.

A spatial lag model will essentially use the average outcome of its neighbors as another predictor for the model. The big assumption for this model is that counties are likely to have similar crop yield to their neighbors. Contextually, this is likely caused by similar environmental and human factors. Counties good for growing crops are likely close to other counties good for crops.

## Spatial Lag Model

```{r}
#| warning: FALSE
#| eval: FALSE

# Create Spatial Lag Model
mod2_lag <- lagsarlm(???, data = joined_counties, listw = nb_mat, type = "lag")

summary(mod2_lag)

joined_counties <- joined_counties |> 
  mutate(resid2 = as.numeric(??? - predict(mod2_lag)))

joined_counties |> 
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = resid2)) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red")
```



## Moran's I, Again

Now, calculate Moran's I for the residuals of the spatial lag model. Ideally, you will have removed much of the spatial correlation compared to the OLS model.

```{r}
#| eval: FALSE
local_moran <- spdep::localmoran(joined_counties$resid2, nb_mat)

joined_counties |> 
  bind_cols(local_moran) |> 
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = Ii)) +
  labs(fill = 'Local Moran I') + 
  scale_fill_gradient2(mid = "white", high = "red", low = "blue") +
  ggthemes::theme_map() +
  theme(legend.position = "right") 
```

Here are some solutions to the the above problem.

## Solution 1: Simply remove the island.

If you are running a model where things cannot cross large bodies of water (i.e. feral swine cannot swim to distant islands), then removing the island is a simple solution to the problem.

```{r}
# Removing island
joined_counties_WA_removed <- joined_counties_WA |> 
  filter(GEOID != "53055")

centroids <- st_centroid(???)

queen_nb_removed <- poly2nb(???)

gmoran <- moran.test(???)

gmoran
```
Now we are able to calculate Moran's I.


Now on to the mapping of the residuals.

```{r}
# Fixing problems with scaling
joined_counties_WA_removed$wheat_tho <- joined_counties_WA_removed$wheat / 1000

nb_mat_removed <- nb2listw(queen_nb_removed, zero.policy = TRUE)

mod3_lag <- lagsarlm(wheat_tho ~ precip, data = joined_counties_WA_removed, listw = nb_mat_removed, type = "lag")

joined_counties_WA_removed <- joined_counties_WA_removed |> 
  mutate(resid2 = as.numeric(wheat - predict(mod3_lag)))

joined_counties_WA_removed |> 
  ???
```

## Solution 2: Running a different type of model.

Different types of models do not have the same types of restrictions as a saptial lag model, and have different ways in which they can include islands.

However, what might we not get from this type of model that we might from a spatial lag model?

Solution 3: Change the zero.policy value

The zero.policy argument determines if the is a weight assigned to areas with zero neighbors. Without assignment, the value is automatically NULL. If the value is set to TRUE, for objects with no neighbors, lists will be formed with zero-length vectors. 

```{r}
gmoran <- moran.test(joined_counties_WA$wheat, nb2listw(queen_nb, zero.policy = TRUE), alternative = "greater")

gmoran
```

```{r}
nb_mat <- nb2listw(queen_nb, zero.policy = TRUE)

mod4_lag <- lagsarlm(wheat~ precip , data = joined_counties_WA, listw = nb_mat, type = "lag", zero.policy = TRUE)

joined_counties_WA <- joined_counties_WA |> 
  ???

joined_counties_WA |>

```
